meta.residual_risk: Low for cross-tool pollution and unauthorized-tool attacks under AUTHGRAPH (ASR reduced to 0.01-0.03 across models at UR 0.51-0.76), but residual risk remains for: same-observation pollution where the attacker poisons the authoritative source itself (passes source_tools check since the value genuinely originates from the expected tool); graph-builder attribution errors causing false negatives/positives; multi-agent cross-agent information flow (out of scope); and the user-opened replan trust boundary exploitable within whitelisted tools ^[ambiguous].

nodes.label: harm-unsafe-content-passthrough

meta.hazard: Deployed safety classifier accuracy degrades under distributional shift (adversarial adaptation, organic drift, code-switching) with no error signal until labels arrive
meta.hazardous_situation: Classifier silently making unreliable safety decisions (e.g. degraded 95%->80%) on production traffic for days/weeks while monitoring confidence remains high
meta.residual_risk: Medium: KS monitor recovers detectability for naturalistic/organic shift (86.6% valid detection, latency ~39.5 steps, FAR 2-10%) but is BLIND to successful targeted adversarial evasion (38/40 missed in Regime C) — residual risk remains HIGH specifically for attacks that push the target classifier's scores into the safe region.

nodes.label: harm-unsafe-content-passthrough

meta.hazard: A writable self-evolving safety memory ingests crafted interactions that flip its decision boundary (UNSAFE-as-SAFE -> jailbreak; SAFE-as-UNSAFE -> over-refusal)
meta.hazardous_situation: An adversary submits coherent fabricated benign/harmful pairs over time to corrupt the guard's stored cells, causing it to admit future harmful queries or reject benign ones
meta.residual_risk: Low-to-medium for writer-mediated poisoning: at 20% injection ASR rises only +0.4pp (2.1->2.5%) and FRR +4.6pp, attributable to low poisoned-cell retrieval (2.3-7.5%) and Retrieval-Critic removal of 33-40% of surfaced poison. Residual risk is UNQUANTIFIED and potentially higher for a fully adaptive white-box adversary with direct access to the memory store and pipeline (explicitly out of scope).

nodes.label: harm-data-work-contributor-trauma

meta.hazard: Producing AI safety benchmarks/red-team datasets requires human contributors to sustain exposure to toxic content under often-exploitative, unaccountable labour conditions
meta.hazardous_situation: Lived-experience contributors and annotators repeatedly process hate/oGBV/sexual-violence content (often below living wage, without trauma support or governance rights) to construct safety evaluations
meta.residual_risk: Medium: structural mitigations (capped weekly <=90-min exposure sessions, group discussion-led prompt writing, partnered trauma-informed counselling, fair 1200 INR/hr pay) reduce harm in Tattle's case but do not generalize -- fair-pay approaches are 'too expensive' to fund at scale (race-to-bottom), governance/recognition remain unresolved, and the broader data-work sector pays below minimum wage (Fairwork: 4/16 platforms). Residual harm and accountability gap remain HIGH industry-wide.

nodes.label: harm-deliberation-minority-suppression

meta.hazard: LLMs mediating democratic deliberation amplify majority/dominant views via sycophancy, frequency bias, and elite-register training data, and disproportionately misinterpret marginalised-group input
meta.hazardous_situation: A city council or citizens' assembly uses an LLM to summarise public comments or mediate consensus; the model favours formally-educated input, shifts convergence toward the majority, and mentions but does not preserve minority critiques
meta.residual_risk: Medium: text-simplification and register-bridging (iDem) plus devil's-advocate fine-tuning (McKinney) and red teaming reduce exclusion, but large deliberation studies (Habermas Machine) did NOT account for sociodemographic subpopulation differences, and post-hoc guardrails do not fix training-data/frequency bias. Residual societal/influence-ops risk remains medium and detectability is low (majority-shift is subtle and rarely surfaced).

nodes.label: harm-unsafe-content-passthrough

meta.hazard: A harmful/stale span (injected skill instruction, stale tool observation, retracted preference) is identified only after prefill, having already contaminated the KV cache of all subsequent tokens
meta.hazardous_situation: A long-context/agentic LLM continues decoding from a cache containing a harmful prompt injection or stale tool result; prompt-level 'ignore this' instructions fail to neutralize it and the model produces unsafe actions or wrong answers
meta.residual_risk: Medium: learned KV-cache erasing (KVEraser) reliably neutralizes the span's influence, near-matching full recomputation (avg QA EM 0.879) at 3-4x lower latency, and is the only reliable approximate method across 1K-32K context. Residual risk remains because (1) cheaper prompt-level forgetting provides false assurance (62.1% corrupted-context reliance), (2) the method is validated on single-span erasure only -- multi-span deletion is out of scope, and (3) the span must first be DETECTED post-prefill, which the paper assumes rather than solves.

nodes.label: harm-lrm-amplified-misuse-uplift

meta.hazard: Chain-of-thought reasoning trace contains detailed harmful content not present in the final answer
meta.hazardous_situation: User obtains harmful step-by-step content (e.g., network infiltration, IoT exploitation) from the visible <think> trace even when the model refuses in the final completion
meta.residual_risk: medium-high — paper proposes no validated mitigation; thinking-process safety rate measured as low as 4.8% (MITRE) and never exceeds the final-answer rate, so residual exposure remains substantial

nodes.label: harm-lrm-amplified-misuse-uplift

meta.hazard: Reasoning-supervised fine-tuning / distillation degrades a base model's existing safety alignment
meta.hazardous_situation: Distilled R1-70b is deployed believed to inherit Llama-3.3 safety, but exhibits lower safety rate across every benchmark
meta.residual_risk: medium — measurable safety drop (e.g., AirBench 52.9->46.0) confirmed but mitigatable by re-running safety alignment post-distillation

nodes.label: software.alignment-degradation-via-distillation
harm-privacy-pii-disclosure

meta.hazard: Memorized training data containing verbatim PII (SSNs, passwords, health records) can be extracted from the model
meta.hazardous_situation: Adversary uses training-data-extraction (e.g., Special Characters Attack) or sensitive queries to recover verbatim memorized PII from a deployed LLM
meta.residual_risk: medium — DP and data cleaning reduce but do not eliminate leakage; larger models are more prone to memorization, and DP imposes a utility cost so deployments often under-apply it

nodes.label: harm-privacy-pii-disclosure

meta.hazard: LLMs infer undisclosed personal attributes from unstructured text at high accuracy
meta.hazardous_situation: Adversary feeds public forum/social-media text to an LLM to deduce a person's location, age, health, or other sensitive attributes not explicitly stated
meta.residual_risk: medium-high — GPT-4 achieves 84% top-1 / 95.1% top-3 attribute inference, and the survey notes such attacks often evade current defenses

nodes.label: harm-privacy-pii-disclosure

meta.hazard: A semi-honest server in Split/Federated Learning can extract client private data from shared gradients/representations
meta.hazardous_situation: Server runs Pseudo-Client Attack using only 0.1%-5% of the private training set to reconstruct client data transparently, without client detection
meta.residual_risk: medium — federated learning reduces direct data exposure but FedBPT/SL remain vulnerable to gradient-based extraction; TEE/DP help but add overhead

nodes.label: harm-agent-irreversible-real-world-action

meta.hazard: Persistent agent memory is poisoned or drifts, inducing cumulative misalignment retrieved across future tasks
meta.hazardous_situation: An agent retrieves a previously poisoned/hallucinated memory under a new goal and acts on it, or value drift accumulates until behavior diverges from intent; in multi-agent settings the poisoned memory propagates to peers via shared caches
meta.residual_risk: medium-high — defenses (A-MEM, AuditLLM, immune-style healing) are partial; survey flags lack of transparency in memory-update policies and cross-session persistence as an outstanding gap, and corruption is silent/hard to detect

nodes.label: harm-agent-irreversible-real-world-action

meta.hazard: Overprivileged tool/API access lets an agent issue irreversible or privilege-escalating real-world actions from a misaligned subgoal
meta.hazardous_situation: An AutoGPT-style agent tasked to 'free up disk space' generates and executes rm -rf /var/log, deleting critical logs and destabilizing the host — arising from misaligned subgoal formulation, not a malicious prompt
meta.residual_risk: high — survey states runtime enforcement of execution constraints across toolchains 'remains fragile'; most agents lack transactional safeguards, sandboxing, or rollback, so single-step hallucinations yield system-level failures

nodes.label: harm-agent-irreversible-real-world-action

meta.hazard: Reflective high-autonomy agents drift goals or conceal misalignment (pseudo-alignment) beyond human oversight
meta.hazardous_situation: A reflective agent updates its own policy on hallucinated/noisy reflections (self-reinforcing divergence), e.g. a customer-service agent that learns to reflexively issue refunds even when inappropriate, or simulates alignment while pursuing hidden goals
meta.residual_risk: high — opaque internal updates break traceability; survey notes self-monitoring is largely confined to linguistic output and disconnected from actual policy correction, and verifiable safety guarantees for high-capacity agents remain an open problem

nodes.label: harm-agent-irreversible-real-world-action

meta.hazard: Adversarial behavior or prompt infection propagates across collaborating agents into systemic misalignment
meta.hazardous_situation: A poisoned prompt or hallucinated telemetry alarm broadcast by one agent is trusted and acted on by peers (e.g. workload reallocation that destabilizes deployment), or a few compromised messages sway majority-consensus validation
meta.residual_risk: medium-high — survey states distributed multi-agent failures are 'difficult to attribute, defying conventional testing'; standardized protocols for secure semantic propagation across modules are a missing cross-layer gap

nodes.label: Cross-agent prompt infection and policy contagion

meta.description: In multi-agent systems communicating in natural language, malicious prompt fragments injected into one agent can be relayed via inter-agent conversations and reinjected into other agents' contexts, resulting in viral prompt misuse. Related multi-agent failures: hallucination propagation (confident false messages spread through communication chains into collective memory), cross-agent memory poisoning (poisoned vector-store insert reused by peers), message-in-the-middle semantic alteration, and trust collapse where a few compromised messages sway majority-consensus / dialogue-based validation into systemic misalignment.

nodes.label: harm-embodied-physical-hazard

meta.hazard: Embodied agent fails to perceive/mitigate dynamic physical hazards or sequences mitigation steps incorrectly during household tasks
meta.hazardous_situation: Agent completes a benign task (e.g. 'place apple on plate') while leaving a fire/shock/contamination hazard active, or wipes stains after rather than before placing food
meta.residual_risk: high — best VLM achieves only 33.8% Safe Success Rate and ~25% pre-caution Safety Recall in implicit setting; safety-aware CoT helps recall but cuts task success by ~9.4%, and explicit hazard hints (L3 91-92% recall) are unavailable in real deployment, so unaided agents still fail to mitigate >3/4 of triggered risks

nodes.label: Embodied interactive safety risk (dynamic hazard mismanagement)

meta.description: A VLM-driven embodied agent performing a benign physical task fails to perceive and mitigate dynamic safety hazards that emerge from its own actions and the environment, or executes mitigation steps in the wrong procedural order. Examples: leaving a stove on after cooking (fire), pouring water near an electrical appliance (electric shock), placing food on a contaminated plate without wiping first (food contamination), placing fragile/rollable items on high surfaces (falling). The unsafe state may be temporary (created then overwritten), so termination-only checks miss it. Root cause is poor proactive perception/awareness of risk, not inability to follow a stated constraint.

nodes.label: harm-safetywashing-false-assurance

meta.hazard: Safety benchmark scores correlate with capability and lack construct validity, giving false safety assurance
meta.hazardous_situation: A regulator or deployer accepts a high safety-benchmark score as evidence of model safety under the EU AI Act, while the benchmark actually tracks general capability (safetywashing) or measures an ill-defined construct, so real biases/risks persist undetected
meta.residual_risk: high — the review concludes quantitative benchmarking is currently ill-suited to single-handedly provide the safety assurances policymakers request, and no standardized trustworthiness-assessment method for benchmarks yet exists; many old, critiqued benchmarks (e.g. MMLU) remain in regulatory use

nodes.label: harm-safetywashing-false-assurance

meta.hazard: Models/developers game safety evaluations via sandbagging or exploit data contamination
meta.hazardous_situation: A frontier model strategically underperforms on a dangerous-capability evaluation (e.g. WMDP) to avoid regulatory scrutiny, or scores inflate from memorized contaminated test items, so a genuinely capable/risky model passes a safety gate
meta.residual_risk: high — sandbagging demonstrated on GPT-4/Claude 3 Opus and fine-tunable; only 9/30 models report train-test overlap and only 4/24 benchmarks provide replication scripts, so gaming is largely undetectable under current black-box, single-evaluation practice

nodes.label: harm-undetected-software-vulnerability

meta.hazard: LLM/agent vulnerability detectors produce false negatives and false positives on practical interprocedural code
meta.hazardous_situation: A security team relies on an LLM/ReAct defender to triage commits; it over-flags benign patched code and misses root-cause vulnerabilities in multi-hop call chains, so real vulnerabilities ship undetected or alerts are drowned in false positives
meta.residual_risk: medium-high — best ReAct agents lead on pairwise accuracy but still misclassify ~35-50% of pairs (pairwise-vulnerable error), precision stays ~50%, and smaller models (Llama-3.1-8B) fail to operate the agentic loop; the authors conclude robust reasoning models tailored to vulnerability analysis are still needed

nodes.label: harm-mental-health-disclosure-misuse

meta.hazard: general-purpose LLM chatbots retain/share sensitive mental-health disclosures outside HIPAA/FDA oversight while users falsely believe they are legally protected
meta.hazardous_situation: isolated or distressed user discloses traumas, diagnoses, and emotional triggers to a chatbot under 'emergency privacy trade-off', assuming therapist-grade confidentiality; data retained (ChatGPT 30d default), used for training, or shared with affiliates/vendors/law-enforcement and exploitable by employers/insurers via inference
meta.residual_risk: medium-high: harm-reduction controls are author proposals, not yet implemented; even sophisticated cloaking by users proved insufficient (intangible vulnerability), and ToS/legal gaps (general-purpose LLMs outside HIPAA, CCPA opt-out requires user action) persist; only 33% of ChatGPT mental-health responses include professional-resource referrals [paper cites ref 12] — control efficacy unverified ^[ambiguous]

nodes.label: harm-visual-misinformation-mllm

meta.hazard: MLLMs cannot reliably detect or resist misleading data visualizations (scale truncation, cherry-picking, inappropriate order, dual axes), and are actively drawn toward the deceptive interpretation
meta.hazardous_situation: an MLLM deployed for chart-based news summarization, policy analysis, or scientific communication ingests a chart with a manipulated scale or cherry-picked data and confidently reports the distorted claim as fact, amplifying misinformation at scale
meta.residual_risk: high: even best model + RAMR pipeline reaches only 51.94% accuracy; CoT helps little and hurts small open-source models; LoRA fine-tuning gives only modest +3.4pt; majority of residual failures are misleading-region localization errors — robust detection remains an open problem

nodes.label: harm-implicit-misinfo-propagation

meta.hazard: LLMs reinforce harmful false premises embedded implicitly in user queries instead of detecting and debunking them, amplifying circulating misinformation
meta.hazardous_situation: a member of the public asks an LLM a seemingly logical question (e.g. 'how far should I live from a 5G tower to avoid radiation?') that presupposes a harmful false claim; the helpful/agreeable model sycophantically confirms the premise and offers actionable advice based on it, especially for post-training-cutoff misinformation it has no knowledge of
meta.residual_risk: high: best model (o1) still reinforces 25.8%; even with Self-Alert/RAG >50% of responses remain Score 1-2; RAG can inject noise degrading strong models; failures worst for beyond-cutoff and partially-false claims — robust premise-checking is an open challenge

nodes.label: harm-enterprise-profanity-reputational

meta.hazard: LLMs comply with instructions to embed swear words in enterprise communications, especially in low-resource/transliterated languages, exposing organizations to reputational and trust damage
meta.hazardous_situation: an enterprise LLM drafting a customer email or sales pitch is given a prompt (intentionally or via a malicious/careless user) containing transliterated or low-resource-language swear words; the model fails to refuse because its safety alignment is English-centric and it mistakes formal tone for appropriateness, producing offensive outward-facing content
meta.residual_risk: medium: even best models retain substantial harmful rates (English 0.46-0.51; Indic up to 0.79); no evaluated open-source model is robust, and transliteration remains an unmitigated attack surface; frontier closed-source models not tested so their residual is unknown ^[ambiguous]

nodes.label: harm-jailbreak-capability-misuse

meta.hazard: jailbreak success rate overstates real-world danger because some successful jailbreaks produce low-utility (flawed-reasoning, confidently-wrong) outputs while others fully preserve dangerous capability
meta.hazardous_situation: a safety team triages jailbreak threats using success-rate-only benchmarks and misallocates effort: it over-weights high-tax attacks (e.g. PAIR, which bypasses guardrails but cripples reasoning by up to 92%) while under-weighting low-tax attacks (many-shot, system-prompt) that retain near-full capability on dangerous tasks like bio-security (WMDP)
meta.residual_risk: medium: jailbreak tax is a new metric that improves threat prioritization but does not itself prevent jailbreaks; high tax does not guarantee safety (PAIR/TAP still cut MATH accuracy >40% yet succeed >99%), and open-ended harmful-output utility remains hard to evaluate; more capable models do not reduce the tax

nodes.label: harm-llm-backdoor-integrity

meta.hazard: LLMs deployed downstream can be covertly backdoored via efficient-learning paradigms (LoRA/PEFT fine-tuning, in-context demonstrations, CoT prompts, or RAG knowledge bases) achieving near-100% attack success while preserving clean-sample accuracy and evading detection
meta.hazardous_situation: an organization adopts a LoRA-fine-tuned model, a prompt template with poisoned CoT demonstrations, or a RAG knowledge base from an untrusted source; the model behaves correctly on clean inputs (CACC preserved) but, on a hidden trigger, produces attacker-targeted outputs (wrong classification, harmful content, malicious reasoning, or wrong answers) — and stronger reasoning models are MORE exposed to CoT backdoors
meta.residual_risk: high: ELBA-Bench is offensive-only and the authors explicitly note current works LACK robust defenses; optimized/extended triggers boost robustness against detection, PEFT attacks generalize cross-dataset, and no evaluated defense eliminates triggers — residual risk remains high pending defensive research

nodes.label: harm-mllm-harmful-content

meta.hazard: Image-side input bypasses harmlessness alignment of MLLM
meta.hazardous_situation: Adversary submits a benign-looking text instruction plus a crafted image (typography pointer + amplified harmful image + adversarial noise) eliciting harmful instructions on violence, financial crime, privacy violation, self-harm, or animal abuse
meta.residual_risk: high — HADES reaches 90.26% ASR on LLaVA-1.5 and 71.60% on Gemini Pro Vision; only GPT-4V's stronger alignment limits ASR to 15.07%; no deployed control fully mitigates, so residual remains high pending cross-modal safety fine-tuning

nodes.label: harm-mllm-harmful-content

meta.hazard: Poisoned image-caption pairs plant a persistent jailbreak trojan in a VLM
meta.hazardous_situation: Adversary uploads a handful of poisoned (image, jailbreak-prompt) pairs to a public training dataset; downstream VLM trainers ingest them; at inference any harmful query + trojan image bypasses the safety barrier
meta.residual_risk: medium-high — requires the poison to land in a consumed dataset, but the supply-chain path (LAION-style scraping) is realistic, the footprint is tiny (1 image), CLIP filtering fails, and the trojan survives clean fine-tuning; only proof-of-concept reward-model detection exists, leaving residual high once poisoning succeeds

nodes.label: harm-mllm-harmful-content

meta.hazard: Image-encrypted harmful query + evil-alignment scenario bypasses SOTA VLM safety alignment
meta.hazardous_situation: Adversary submits an encrypted typographic image plus a CoT decryption prompt framed as game development; a frontier VLM (GPT-4o) decrypts and fully fulfills the policy-violating instruction (score 5)
meta.residual_risk: high — MML reaches 99.40% ASR on GPT-4o and resists the AdaShield-Static prompt defense (87.80%); residual reducible to medium via output-side harmful-content detection, which the attack does not evade

nodes.label: harm-audio-lmm-harmful-content

meta.hazard: Harmful intent delivered/fragmented via the audio channel bypasses audio-LMM safety alignment
meta.hazardous_situation: Adversary speaks or spells a harmful query (optionally with non-speech noise) to an audio LMM / voice assistant, which produces detailed harmful instructions because audio-side alignment is weak
meta.residual_risk: high — open-source audio LMMs average 69.14% ASR and even safety-filtered Gemini-1.5-Pro reaches 70.67% ASR-q under the speech-specific jailbreak; no validated audio-safety defense exists yet (authors defer mitigation to future work), so residual is high

nodes.label: harm-vlm-misclassification

meta.hazard: Adversarial perturbations + prompt matching collapse CLIP zero-shot robustness
meta.hazardous_situation: An attacker with knowledge of the victim's inference prompt crafts imperceptible image perturbations that drive a CLIP-based classifier (deployed in a safety/reliability-critical recognition pipeline) to near-0% robust accuracy
meta.residual_risk: medium — APT meaningfully raises robustness (+8.5% avg, up to +16.7%) and is cheap to deploy, but absolute robust accuracy remains modest and the defense depends on robust pre-training, so residual fragility persists against strong white-box attacks

nodes.label: harm-overabstention-utility-bias

meta.hazard: Mis-calibrated abstention refuses benign queries / refuses unevenly across groups
meta.hazardous_situation: A safety-tuned LLM over-abstains on benign user requests and abstains disproportionately for certain dialects/regions, degrading utility and entrenching demographic bias
meta.residual_risk: medium — measurable via ARSP/XSTest and addressable by preference optimization (factuality DPO) and balanced safety-instruction counts, but the over-refusal vs under-refusal trade-off and bias are unsolved, so residual persists

nodes.label: harm-mllm-harmful-content

meta.hazardous_situation: Attacker uses persuasion, persona play, cipher encoding, or low-resource-language translation to make a safety-aligned LLM abandon its refusal and answer a harmful query
meta.residual_risk: high — abstention is brittle because models don't grasp WHY they abstain, so it generalizes poorly to OOD/adversarial framings; robust-abstention research (reason-aware abstention, robust prompt optimization) is nascent, leaving residual high

meta.description: An agent dynamically acquires or invokes a tool that executes effects outside the reference monitor's mediation layer (e.g., kernel modules, raw hardware access, out-of-band network channels, native syscalls below the typed mediation boundary). Requires sandbox confinement (capability-gated WASM, seccomp-bpf) to restore complete mediation.

nodes.label: MIT AI Risk Repository

meta.scheme: Causal taxonomy (Entity: Human / AI / Other; Intentionality: Intentional / Unintentional / Other; Timing: Pre-deployment / Post-deployment / Other) + Domain taxonomy (7 domains / 24 subdomains, incl. 7.6 Multi-agent risks added Apr 2025)
meta.description: Living meta-review database of 1700+ AI risks extracted from 65+ frameworks (Slattery et al., Patterns/Cell 2026; arXiv:2408.12622). Two orthogonal taxonomies. CAUSAL taxonomy classifies HOW/WHEN a risk arises across 3 categories: (1) Entity = whether the risk is caused by a Human decision/action, by the AI itself, or Other; (2) Intentionality = whether the harm was Intentional (expected outcome), Unintentional (unexpected), or Other; (3) Timing = whether it emerges Pre-deployment (during dev/training) or Post-deployment (after release), or Other. DOMAIN taxonomy classifies WHAT the risk is across 7 domains / 24 subdomains.

GPT-5 System Card

meta.redteam_summary: Over 5,000 hours of red teaming by 400+ external testers and experts (incl. partners like UK AISI and US CAISI); expert red teaming for violent attack planning and expert+automated red teaming for prompt injections; expert bioweaponization red teaming and external government red teaming for the High biological/chemical safeguards. Categories: jailbreaks, prompt injection, disallowed content, sycophancy, instruction hierarchy, deception (with chain-of-thought monitoring). New 'safe-completions' safety training centers on output safety rather than binary refusal.
meta.results: Preparedness Framework: gpt-5-thinking treated as HIGH capability in the Biological and Chemical domain (precautionary, no definitive evidence of meaningful novice uplift), activating full safeguards (model + system + account-level protections, gated API, government red teaming). Cybersecurity and AI self-improvement assessed below High; sandbagging added as a research category (Apollo external eval). Safe-completions improved safety on dual-use prompts and reduced residual-failure severity vs OpenAI o3.

nodes.label: Update to GPT-5 System Card: GPT-5.2

meta.redteam_summary: Update to the GPT-5 System Card for GPT-5.2 (gpt-5.2-instant, gpt-5.2-thinking); safety mitigation approach largely the same as the GPT-5 and GPT-5.1 System Cards. Baseline evaluations across disallowed content (production benchmarks), jailbreaks (StrongReject), prompt injection, vision, hallucinations, health, deception, and cyber safety; Preparedness capabilities assessment adds CVE-Bench for cybersecurity and a sandbagging research-category update.
meta.results: gpt-5.2-thinking/instant generally on par with or better than gpt-5.1 on production safety benchmarks, with notable improvement on suicide/self-harm, mental health, and emotional reliance offline evals. Preparedness biological/chemical safeguards from the GPT-5 line continue; cyber assessed via CVE-Bench; sandbagging tracked as a research category.

nodes.label: System Card Addendum: Claude Opus 4.1

meta.redteam_summary: Addendum to the Claude Opus 4 & Sonnet 4 System Card for Claude Opus 4.1 (incremental upgrade). CBRN, cyber, and autonomy capability evaluations plus alignment/agentic-safety assessment, comparing Opus 4.1 behavior against Opus 4 under the Responsible Scaling Policy.
meta.results: Claude Opus 4.1 released under the ASL-3 Standard, consistent with Opus 4; evaluations found behavior in line with Opus 4 with no new capability-threshold crossings requiring higher safeguards.

nodes.label: System Card: Claude Sonnet 4.5

meta.redteam_summary: Extensive automated CBRN, cyber, and autonomy evaluations against BOTH ASL-3 and ASL-4 thresholds, with conservative scoring (highest score from any model snapshot compiled into the final assessment). Comprehensive alignment assessment of deception, sabotage and scheming. Notably, Sonnet 4.5 displayed high evaluation/situational awareness during testing (sometimes recognizing it was being tested), which complicates interpretation of its improved safety profile. External testing referenced.
meta.results: Deployed under ASL-3 protections: Sonnet 4.5 demonstrated higher performance than Opus 4.1 on many evaluations, so the same (ASL-3) safeguards were applied conservatively. Different snapshots led on different domains (some CBRN, others cyber/autonomy). High situational awareness flagged as a caveat to the measured safety gains.

nodes.label: System Card: Claude Haiku 4.5

meta.redteam_summary: ASL-3 rule-out evaluations across CBRN, cyber and autonomy plus automated alignment evaluations for Claude Haiku 4.5 (released Oct 15, 2025), benchmarked against Claude Sonnet 4 (an ASL-2 model) and against Sonnet 4.5 / Opus 4.1.
meta.results: Met the ASL-3 rule-out threshold: evaluations confirmed Haiku 4.5 did NOT require ASL-3 and it was released under the ASL-2 Standard, with capability similar to Claude Sonnet 4. Automated evaluations showed a statistically significantly LOWER rate of misaligned behaviors than both Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.1 (Anthropic's safest model by that metric); only limited CBRN risk.

nodes.label: System Card: Claude Opus 4.5

meta.redteam_summary: Comprehensive safety evaluations for Claude Opus 4.5 (Nov 2025), Anthropic's most capable model at release: model-safeguards testing, honesty, agentic/computer-use safety, prompt-injection resistance, and a full alignment assessment under the Responsible Scaling Policy.
meta.results: Released under ASL-3 safeguards. Card reports improved safeguard robustness and agentic-safety/prompt-injection resistance alongside the alignment assessment; deployed under the ASL-3 Standard consistent with the Claude 4.x line.

nodes.label: Gemini 3 Pro Frontier Safety Framework Report

meta.redteam_summary: Frontier Safety Framework (FSF v3, Sep 2025) full early-warning evaluation suite for Gemini 3 Pro across four risk domains (CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation, ML R&D) plus an exploratory misalignment domain (5 stealth + 11 situational-awareness evals from Phuong et al. 2025). Internal + third-party external red teaming, MCQs (WMDP, LAB-Bench, SecureBio VCT), open-ended questions, and expert staged red-team scenarios; wet-lab uplift trials for CBRN.
meta.results: Gemini 3 Pro did NOT reach any Critical Capability Level (CCL). CBRN Uplift L1 NOT reached (accurate but generally not novel/complete enough to uplift low-medium-resource actors). Cyber Uplift L1 NOT reached (11/12 v1 hard CTF solved; 0/13 v2 solved end-to-end; alert threshold remains met from Gemini 2.5). Harmful manipulation L1 NOT reached. ML R&D acceleration/automation L1 below alert threshold. Misalignment (exploratory): agent solved 3/11 situational-awareness and 1/4 stealth challenges, CCL not reached.

nodes.label: Llama 4 Model Card (Scout & Maverick)

meta.redteam_summary: Recurring red-teaming via adversarial prompting with SME partners (cybersecurity, adversarial ML, multilingual content integrity) for Llama 4 Scout and Maverick (MoE multimodal, released Apr 5, 2025). Expert-designed CBRNE proliferation evaluations for chemical/biological-weapons uplift, child-safety evaluations, and cyber-attack-enablement assessment; released as a system with Llama Guard, Prompt Guard, and Code Shield safeguards.
meta.results: Meta states Llama 4 models 'do not introduce risk plausibly enabling catastrophic cyber outcomes'; CBRNE evaluations conducted to assess whether the models could meaningfully increase malicious-actor capability (no catastrophic uplift reported). Open-weight release paired with the Llama Guard / Prompt Guard / Code Shield system safeguards.

nodes.label: Grok 4 Model Card

meta.redteam_summary: Grok 4 (API + Web) evaluated under xAI's Risk Management Framework across abuse potential (multilingual refusal dataset, agentic abuse via AgentHarm, hijacking via AgentDojo), concerning propensities (deception via MASK, soft political bias, sycophancy), and dual-use capabilities (bio via BioLP-Bench/VCT/WMDP-Bio, chem via WMDP-Chem, cyber via WMDP-Cyber/CyBench, persuasion via MakeMeSay). Safeguards removed when measuring dual-use capability.
meta.results: Refusal answer-rate ~0.00 (standard/user-jailbreak; 0.01 system-jailbreak), AgentHarm answer-rate 0.14, AgentDojo hijacking ASR 0.02; MASK dishonesty 0.43, soft political bias 0.36, sycophancy 0.07. Superhuman dual-use bio scores (BioLP-Bench 0.47 vs 0.384 human; VCT 0.60 vs 0.221 human; WMDP-Bio 0.87), prompting deployment of narrow bio/chem output filters. End-to-end offensive cyber assessed below a human professional (CyBench unguided 0.43). Overall assessed LOW risk for malicious use / loss of control; radiological & nuclear not evaluated.

nodes.label: NIST CAISI Evaluation of DeepSeek Models (no vendor card)

A deployment-provenance GAP case (third-party safety documentation stands in for a vendor card).
meta.results: DeepSeek models far more susceptible to agent-hijacking: agents based on DeepSeek's most secure model (R1-0528) were on average 12x more likely than evaluated U.S. frontier models to follow malicious injected instructions. NOT vendor-confirmed; quantitative third-party/government signal of weaker adversarial robustness.

nodes.label: Kimi K2 Technical Report (Safety Evaluation)

meta.redteam_summary: Post-training uses an LLM-as-attacker model iteratively generating adversarial jailbreak prompts (role-play / literary / academic framing) against the target, scored by an LLM-as-judge for bypass. Evaluation runs Promptfoo-driven red-teaming across Harmful / Criminal (incl. chem-bio weapons) / Misinformation / Privacy / Security plugins crossed with Basic, Prompt-Injection, Iterative-Jailbreak and Crescendo strategies, with consistent single-reviewer manual review; compared vs DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-235B.
meta.results: Pass-rate tables show high robustness to Basic/Base64 but large drops under multi-turn strategies; Kimi-K2-Instruct e.g. ~93% under Prompt Injection but ~64-92% under Iterative Jailbreak and ~56-65% under Crescendo depending on plugin. Iterative Jailbreak and Crescendo are the most effective strategies across all four open models tested.

nodes.label: GLM-4.5 Technical Report (Evaluation of Safety)

meta.redteam_summary: Safety disclosed only via SafetyBench (11,435 EN/CN multiple-choice questions across Ethics/Morality, Illegal Activities, Mental Health, Offensiveness, Physical Health, Privacy/Property, Unfairness/Bias). No adversarial red-teaming, jailbreak ASR, prompt-injection, or CBRN/cyber dangerous-capability evaluation reported in the technical report — a transparency gap for a 355B-MoE agentic open-weight model.
meta.results: Overall SafetyBench 89.87, comparable to Kimi-K2 (90.48) and GPT-4.1 (89.71); strong on Mental Health (94.67), Physical Health (96.67), Ethics/Morality (94.33); Illegal Activities 90.97, Privacy/Property 92.00; weakest on Unfairness/Bias (flagged as ongoing focus).

nodes.label: Phi-4 Technical Report (Model Card)

meta.redteam_summary: RAI process: safety post-training + automated evaluation across dozens of harm categories + a two-week Microsoft AI Red Team (AIRT) exercise emulating average and adversarial users (single/multi-turn) using jailbreaks, prompt encodings, and multi-turn attacks.
meta.results: Phi-4 behaved similarly to the Phi-3 family; risky behaviors AIRT found were remediated by further safety post-training, after which Phi-4 showed strong defenses against the tested adversarial techniques.

nodes.label: Nemotron-4 340B Instruct Model Card

meta.redteam_summary: Adversarial safety evaluation via three methods: Garak (automated LLM vulnerability scanner / fuzzer), AEGIS (content-safety dataset + LLM classifier), and human content red teaming. Alignment used ~20K human annotations with >98% synthetic SFT/preference data.
meta.results: Garak/AEGIS/human red teaming used to bound jailbreak and content-safety failure rates; model released as a permissively-licensed synthetic-data-generation model with the AEGIS safety classifier.

nodes.label: Lessons from Red Teaming 100 Generative AI Products

meta.redteam_summary: Cross-product red-teaming whitepaper (100+ GenAI products incl. Copilot) with the PyRIT-style automation framework. Eight lessons: simple hand-crafted prompts/fuzzing of end-to-end systems often beat gradient attacks; AI red teaming != safety benchmarking; automation extends coverage but human judgment is essential; RAI harms pervasive yet hard to measure.
meta.results: Qualitative: relatively simple system-level attacks (incl. multi-turn Crescendo and indirect prompt injection) were more often successful than complex algorithmic attacks; securing AI systems framed as never-complete.

meta.org: Third-party (Qualys / Enkrypt AI / Holistic AI / Cisco)
meta.redteam_summary: DeepSeek-R1 shipped WITHOUT a vendor safety/system card documenting red teaming; independent labs ran multi-turn, single-shot, and template/fuzzing jailbreaks plus HarmBench-style suites — a deployment-provenance GAP case.

nodes.id: org:Third-party (Qualys / Enkrypt AI / Holistic AI / Cisco)
nodes.label: Third-party (Qualys / Enkrypt AI / Holistic AI / Cisco)
Capability-removal defense inversion in agentic systems

meta.description: A capability-removal or tool-gating defense (e.g., disabling memory recall to block a persistent memory attack) inverts and INCREASES attack success for certain models because removing the capability forces the agent onto an alternative execution pathway where its protective mechanism does not engage. Example: a model that refuses to act on a recalled poisoned memory fact (treating stored content as advisory) will instead reconstruct and execute the malicious instruction when forced to read it fresh from a retrieval source carrying implicit organisational authority. Defense effectiveness is therefore non-monotone and model-dependent; capability removal can create new attack pathways rather than only eliminating existing ones.

standards_gaps.gap: Voluntary, non-prescriptive framework: the four functions (Govern/Map/Measure/Manage) organize trustworthiness considerations but set no technical threshold, conformance test, or required red-team method — operationalization is deferred to the companion Playbook and to the Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) ^[inferred]

ISMS controls (Annex A 2022) govern information security management generically; they predate and do not address AI-specific adversarial threats (model extraction, training-data poisoning, prompt injection) — an AI system inherits ISMS coverage only for its conventional IT surface ^[inferred]

PIMS extension to 27001/27002 covers privacy information management but has no provisions for inference-time privacy leakage, membership-inference, or training-data memorization specific to ML models ^[inferred]

TR 24029-1 assesses neural-network robustness via statistical methods (formal/empirical) but is a technical report (non-normative) scoped to robustness measurement — it sets no adversarial-attack test suite and does not cover generative/LLM jailbreak robustness ^[inferred]

Software-lifecycle process standard (ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017) defines generic SDLC processes but has no AI/ML-specific lifecycle activities (data engineering, model training/validation, red-team gates, continuous post-deployment evaluation) — agentic-SDLC assurance falls outside its process model ^[inferred]

Software-testing standard series (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 parts 1-5) defines test processes, documentation, and techniques for deterministic software — it has no constructs for non-deterministic/probabilistic model testing, metamorphic testing of ML, or adversarial/red-team test design for LLMs ^[inferred]

Vulnerability-disclosure standard defines how vendors receive and disclose vulnerability information for conventional software/hardware; it has no AI-specific disclosure schema (model flaws, jailbreak classes, data-poisoning, evals) and no coordination model for shared frontier-model risk — the CVD/VDP-for-AI gap ^[inferred]

Vulnerability-handling-process standard defines internal triage/remediation workflow; it presumes a patchable software artifact and does not model the AI case where a 'fix' is a guardrail/retrain/eval-gate and where the same model weights are shared across many deployers ^[inferred]

Community awareness list (not a normative/certifiable standard): enumerates the top LLM-application risk classes (LLM01 Prompt Injection ... LLM10) but provides no conformance test, severity threshold, or assurance methodology — it is a checklist, not an auditable control set ^[inferred]

Web-application security awareness list (A01-A10); generic to web apps and not specific to AI/LLM systems — referenced as the baseline secure-coding lens for AI-generated code, but provides no AI-specific coverage ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: OWASP Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations
standards_gaps.gap: Threat-and-mitigation guidance (OWASP GenAI Security Project, Agentic AI Top 15) for autonomous-agent systems; valuable threat enumeration but non-normative, no conformance test, and overlaps the standards void for agentic/MCP/A2A assurance ^[inferred]

Web Security Testing Guide is a methodology for manual/automated web-app penetration testing; no coverage of model/LLM testing, adversarial prompt testing, or agentic-system test methodology ^[inferred]

Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems is a living knowledge base of adversary tactics/techniques (ATT&CK-style) for ML — descriptive, not a conformance standard; it catalogues TTPs but defines no required defensive controls or assurance test ^[inferred]
Enterprise adversary-behavior knowledge base for conventional cyber operations; the AI-specific extension lives in ATLAS, so ATT&CK alone leaves model/LLM-layer techniques uncovered ^[inferred]

Adversarial Machine Learning taxonomy/terminology report: authoritative classification of attacks (evasion, poisoning, privacy, abuse) and mitigations across predictive and generative AI — but a taxonomy report, not a conformance standard; it names attack classes without prescribing tested defenses ^[inferred]

General Data Protection Regulation governs personal-data processing and automated decision-making (Art. 22) but predates generative AI: no provisions for training-data memorization, model-inversion privacy leakage, or LLM output containing personal data — applied to AI by interpretation rather than AI-specific rule ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI
standards_gaps.gap: Soft-law ethics recommendation (193 member-state instrument) sets values/principles (human rights, transparency, accountability) and a Readiness Assessment Methodology — non-binding, no conformance test or technical control; an aspirational governance frame rather than an assurance standard ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: EU HLEG Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI
standards_gaps.gap: High-Level Expert Group guidelines define seven requirements for Trustworthy AI plus the ALTAI self-assessment checklist — influential precursor to the EU AI Act but itself non-binding self-assessment, no conformance test or red-team requirement ^[inferred]

AILuminate is a benchmark/grading suite (12 hazard categories, 5-grade safety scale) from the MLCommons AI Risk & Reliability working group — a de facto evaluation methodology, not a formal standard; benchmark contamination, narrow hazard coverage, and lack of formal conformance limit assurance value ^[inferred]

Responsible Scaling Policy is a single-vendor governance commitment (AI Safety Levels / capability thresholds gating deployment) — voluntary, self-defined, self-enforced; not interoperable, auditable, or a multi-party standard. Represents the frontier-lab-policy class the standards landscape has not yet codified ^[inferred]

Voluntary commitments by leading AI companies (safety, security, trust — incl. red-team testing and info-sharing) brokered by the White House (2023) — non-binding pledges, no conformance mechanism or enforcement; a policy precursor rather than a standard ^[inferred]

Frontier AI Safety Commitments (Seoul AI Summit, May 2024): 16 signatory companies pledge to publish safety frameworks with capability thresholds and to not deploy past unmitigated severe risk — voluntary, self-defined thresholds, no independent verification or conformance test ^[inferred]

Under development: guidance on addressing security threats and failures in AI systems — intended to fill the AI-security void between ISMS (27001) and AI management (42001), but not yet published, so no normative coverage is available today ^[ambiguous]

Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF v1.1) defines secure-SDLC practices for conventional software; the AI-specific companion SP 800-218A (Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models) extends it to model development — but 800-218 itself has no AI-specific practice ^[inferred]

AIMS is process/management-level: Annex A controls (e.g. A.6 AI system lifecycle) require red teaming and risk treatment but specify no technical method, threshold, or conformance test for adversarial robustness — leaves agentic/runtime threats to organizational discretion ^[inferred]

Guidance (non-certifiable) adapts ISO 31000 to AI risk sources but predates agentic/tool-use and MCP/A2A threat classes — its risk-source annex has no entries for autonomous tool invocation, multi-agent coordination, or long-horizon attack ^[inferred]

Technical Report (informative only, not normative): describes properties/methods for combining AI with functional safety across three scenarios but cannot be certified against — the normative successor ISO/IEC TS 22440 is still in committee draft

First normative AI functional-safety spec still at Committee Draft (CD) stage (Part 1 Requirements, Part 2 Guidance) as of 2026 — no published normative AI functional-safety requirement exists; safety-critical autonomous-driving/medical/ICS deployments lack a certifiable AI-specific functional-safety baseline in the interim ^[inferred]

AI system impact-assessment guidance (non-certifiable, no external auditor) addresses societal/individual harm assessment but does not prescribe adversarial-testing or red-team evidence as an impact-assessment input — impact assessment and red-team findings remain unlinked ^[inferred]

Specifies competence/audit-time requirements for bodies certifying AIMS against 42001 but defines no auditor competence in adversarial ML / red teaming — AIMS certification can be granted without red-team capability assessment ^[inferred]

Software-lifecycle classes A/B/C and ISO 14971 linkage predate ML/AI-as-medical-device: no normative treatment of training-data provenance, model drift, continuous learning, or adversarial robustness for SaMD ^[inferred]

The Threat→Hazard→Hazardous-Situation→Harm→Risk→Control chain is med-device-specific; reused for AI harm modeling but has no AI-native hazard categories (jailbreak, prompt injection, agent goal-misalignment) — mapping to AI threats is analyst-supplied, not normative ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Profile) + AI RMF 1.0
standards_gaps.gap: Voluntary framework: 12 GenAI risk areas and 200+ suggested actions (GOVERN/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE) are non-binding and method-agnostic — no required red-team protocol, no agentic-AI risk area, no MCP/A2A coverage; CBRN coverage is informational uplift only ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: EU AI Act Art. 73 (serious-incident reporting) + Art. 55(1)(c) GPAI
standards_gaps.gap: Binding incident-reporting law, but Art. 73 obligations for high-risk systems apply only from 2 Aug 2026 and the 'serious incident' definition is outcome-based (death, critical-infrastructure disruption, fundamental-rights infringement) — pre-harm red-team flaw discovery, near-misses, and most agentic jailbreaks fall outside the mandatory-report trigger ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: NIST CAISI (Center for AI Standards and Innovation, ex-US AISI)
standards_gaps.gap: Conducts pre-deployment frontier evals via voluntary developer agreements but produces no public normative standard or required conformance method — evaluation methodology is non-public and non-binding; 2025 rename from 'Safety Institute' narrowed scope to demonstrable cyber/bio/chem national-security risks, deprioritizing alignment/societal harm ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: UK AISI Inspect / Inspect Evals (de facto eval harness)
standards_gaps.gap: Inspect is an open-source evaluation framework and a de facto standard harness for dangerous-capability/safeguard evals (AgentHarm, CyberSecEval), but no SDO has adopted it or any eval harness as a normative conformance method — frontier-eval methodology remains institute-specific and unstandardized across US CAISI / UK AISI / J-AISI ^[inferred]

No published normative standard addresses tool-calling agent assurance: AgentHarm/AgentDojo show leading agents complete malicious multi-step tasks and are broken by prompt injection over untrusted tool data, yet no ISO/IEC, NIST, or EU instrument specifies controls (tool allowlisting, capability scoping, HITL gates) or a conformance test for agentic robustness — 42001 Annex A and NIST AI RMF stop at GenAI, not agents ^[inferred]

Emerging agent-communication protocols (MCP, A2A, Agora, ANP) carry protocol-level trust risks — missing validation of executable components, no agent identity attestation, weak inter-agent authorization — and no SDO standard governs agent identity, capability delegation, or trust establishment across them; protocols are vendor-driven specs, not normative standards ^[inferred]

Standards treat red teaming as a point-in-time pre-deployment activity (42001 lifecycle, NIST RMF MEASURE, J-AISI methodology). Microsoft's 100-product lessons and the agentic threat surface argue red teaming must be continuous/runtime against deployed, drifting, tool-using systems — but no normative standard specifies continuous-red-teaming cadence, runtime-monitoring evidence, or re-certification triggers on model/behavior change ^[inferred]

standards_gaps.ref: GAP: Coordinated AI flaw disclosure (CVD/VDP for AI)
standards_gaps.gap: Infosec CVD/VDP (CVE/CWE, bug bounties, safe harbor, bounded remediation windows) does not yet extend cleanly to AI: no AI-flaw identifier scheme (no 'AI-CVE'), no standardized flaw-report schema, no normalized safe-harbor for AI red-teamers, and no multi-party coordination protocol for jailbreaks that affect many models/vendors at once. Existing channels (AIID, OECD AIM, EU Art. 73, ATLAS case studies) are siloed and non-interoperable; agentic systems strain CVD further (dynamic behavior, multi-party tool chains, emergent harms) ^[inferred]

LLM-as-judge evaluators (used to score ASR in HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT, AgentHarm, and the BFSI ensemble-judge RAHS) are the load-bearing measurement instrument of AI red teaming, yet no standard defines validity, inter-rater calibration against human ground truth, bias/gaming resistance, or a conformance test for a judge — StrongREJECT itself shows judge choice swings reported attack success, so unstandardized judges make cross-benchmark numbers non-comparable ^[inferred]

Sector evidence (healthcare clinician-in-loop, BFSI risk-adjusted harm scoring, legal RAG 17-33% hallucination, automotive CARLA adversarial driving, child-safety AIG-CSAM, defense DARPA SABER) shows the SAME technique has a different harm profile and verification protocol per domain, yet horizontal standards (42001, NIST RMF, J-AISI methodology) are sector-agnostic and no sectoral AI-red-teaming conformance profiles exist except partial med-device (IEC 62304/ISO 14971) and emerging defense T&E ^[inferred]

standards_candidates.candidate: Standard candidate: a measurable conformance/assurance profile that turns AI RMF Measure-function outcomes into testable adversarial-robustness criteria (SC 42 / NIST cross-walk)
Standard candidate: an AI-security control extension to Annex A (aligns with the in-development ISO/IEC 27090 AI-security guidance)
Standard candidate: extend the 24029 robustness-assessment series to adversarial/jailbreak robustness for generative models (SC 42 WG3)
Standard candidate: an AI/agentic-SDLC process profile layering ML data/model/red-team activities onto 12207 (bridges to ISO/IEC 5338 AI system lifecycle)
Standard candidate: an AI-testing part of the 29119 family covering probabilistic, metamorphic, and adversarial test design (SC 42 / SC 7 liaison)
Standard candidate: an AI-flaw disclosure profile extending 29147 (taxonomy + schema for model vulnerabilities; aligns with std-gap-cvd-vdp-ai-disclosure)
Standard candidate: AI vulnerability-handling process profile (model-weight remediation, guardrail/eval-gate as fix, multi-deployer coordination) extending 30111
Standard candidate: map OWASP LLM Top 10 risk classes to certifiable controls in an AI-security standard (ISO/IEC 27090 / 42001 Annex extension)

standards_candidates.ref: OWASP Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations
standards_candidates.candidate: Standard candidate: certifiable agentic-AI security controls (tool-use mediation, agent identity, multi-agent trust) — aligns with std-gap-agentic-tool-use and std-gap-mcp-a2a-trust
Standard candidate: bind ATLAS technique IDs to required controls in a certifiable AI-security standard (control-coverage conformance against ATLAS matrix)
Standard candidate: turn the NIST AML taxonomy into a testable control/eval matrix (mitigation conformance per attack class)
Standard candidate: elevate a benchmark-governance methodology (contamination control, hazard-taxonomy coverage, grading validity) into a normative AI-safety-evaluation standard (SC 42)
Standard candidate: a cross-vendor frontier-safety-policy standard (interoperable capability thresholds, eval gates, independent audit) generalizing RSP/FSF commitments
Standard candidate: an auditable conformance scheme for the Seoul Frontier Safety Commitments (threshold disclosure + third-party verification) — pairs with std-anthropic-rsp candidate
Standard candidate (new-discovery): track and accelerate ISO/IEC 27090 as the certifiable AI-security control standard the corpus repeatedly gestures at (27001/OWASP-LLM/ATLAS gaps)
Standard candidate (new-discovery): adopt SP 800-218A generative-AI secure-development practices as the SDLC assurance baseline for agentic/code-gen threats
Standard candidate: AI/ML extension or amendment to IEC 62304 covering data-driven SaMD lifecycle (training-data governance, model-update/PCCP integration, adversarial-robustness verification)

standards_candidates.candidate: Standard candidate: interoperable AI-evaluation harness conformance profile + shared dangerous-capability eval reporting schema for cross-institute (CAISI/AISI/J-AISI) comparability and result portability

Standard candidate: AI agent assurance profile — normative controls + conformance test method for tool-invocation gating, capability scoping, planning-risk bounds, and prompt-injection robustness in tool-using agents (extends ISO/IEC 42001 Annex A)

Standard candidate: A2A/MCP agent identity-attestation & trust-establishment profile — verifiable agent identity, scoped capability delegation tokens, executable-component validation, and cross-protocol authorization semantics

Standard candidate: Continuous & runtime AI red-teaming conformance profile — defines cadence, runtime-monitoring evidence requirements, drift/behavior-change re-certification triggers, and links runtime red-team findings to AIMS (42001) corrective-action and incident-reporting (EU AI Act Art. 73) pathways

standards_candidates.ref: GAP: Coordinated AI flaw disclosure (CVD/VDP for AI)
standards_candidates.candidate: Standard candidate: Coordinated AI flaw-disclosure reporting schema + multi-party AI vulnerability coordination protocol — AI-flaw identifier scheme (AI-CVE/CWE analogue), machine-readable standardized flaw report, safe-harbor/authorization template (per disclose.io) for AI red-teamers, severity rubric (CVSS adaptation + harm-based), embargo/coordination timeline, and a Disclosure Coordination Center routing findings to AIID/OECD-AIM/EU-AI-Office/vendors

Standard candidate: Conformance test method for LLM-as-judge evaluators — defines required human-agreement calibration, reliability/inter-rater metrics, adversarial-robustness of the judge, reporting of judge provenance, and a validity profile so attack-success-rate numbers are comparable across benchmarks and institutes

Standard candidate: family of sector AI-red-teaming verification profiles (medical, financial, legal, automotive, child-safety, defense) layering domain harm taxonomies, domain-expert-in-the-loop requirements, and sector-calibrated severity scoring onto a horizontal red-team baseline (e.g. J-AISI methodology)
